title: Plan to triple adaptation finance kept off COP31's formal agenda
excerpt: Without its own agenda item there is no negotiating track to define or track the pledge, which Bangladesh and African countries want.

image.alt: A coastal embankment curving along a river beside mangroves and a small settlement in Bangladesh

content:
A proposal to give the pledge to triple adaptation finance its own item on the COP31 agenda failed to win consensus at the summit’s opening session in Antalya, allAfrica reported on 12 November. COP31 President Murat Kurum ruled that the issue could be discussed under existing agenda items instead.

The African Group of Negotiators (AGN) had pressed for a dedicated agenda item since the Bonn climate talks in June. The European Union had signalled before the summit that it would not accept one. After the request, the EU and the United Kingdom restated climate finance commitments they had already made, the report said.

Why the agenda item mattered

  • Countries agreed at COP30 in Belém to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035, but did not agree a baseline. The AGN’s chair, Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, said: “Without trajectory, you will not be able to track progress being made.”
  • If the Glasgow Climate Pact baseline is used, international adaptation finance would reach $85 billion to $120 billion a year by 2035. The UN Environment Programme’s Adaptation Gap Report 2026 says that would cover only 20% to 29% of developing countries’ needs, adjusted for inflation, according to the report.
  • Public adaptation finance from developed to developing countries was $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024.

Without its own agenda item, there is no formal negotiating track at COP31 to define, monitor or enforce the tripling pledge. The AGN now wants the target given priority in the cover text, the political declaration adopted by consensus at the end of the summit.

Bangladesh’s position

Bangladesh has backed the tripling goal and went further on 12 November. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman asked that at least half of all international climate finance go to adaptation, as grants rather than loans.

Why it matters

Adaptation money pays for much of what NGOs do in coastal, flood-prone and drought-hit Bangladesh. Without an agreed baseline and a way to track it, the tripling pledge is hard to hold donors to. NGOs and networks that brief the Bangladesh delegation, or work with the Least Developed Countries group, can push for clear tripling language and a baseline in the cover text.

What to watch

  • Whether the COP31 cover text names a baseline or a timeline for tripling adaptation finance.
  • Whether adaptation finance comes up under other agenda items, such as the Global Goal on Adaptation.
